questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes product data 'master data' rather than transactional data?
options: The product record stays the same regardless of how many units sell in a given period
It is recalculated every time a sale occurs
It only exists after a product is discontinued
It is generated automatically from shipping records
questions.explain: A product's name, unit of measure, GTIN, and classification don't change whether it sells one unit or ten thousand — that stability is what makes it master data.

questions.q: What is the difference between a product and a SKU, as explained in this lesson?
options: A product is the conceptual item; a SKU is one specific sellable variant of it with its own barcode and inventory count
A product and a SKU are two words for exactly the same thing
A SKU is always a higher-level grouping than a product
A product only exists in e-commerce, while a SKU only exists in warehouses
questions.explain: 'Men's Crew Socks, Size M' is the product; 'Men's Crew Socks, Size M, Black, 3-Pack' is a SKU — one of possibly many variants under that product.

questions.q: What practical problem occurs if a product master only tracks the product level and not the SKU level?
options: A warehouse can't tell which specific barcode to pick off the shelf
The product automatically becomes discontinued
Customers are no longer able to purchase the item at all
The product's brand classification disappears
questions.explain: Inventory and fulfillment operate at the SKU level — the specific color, size, or pack — so collapsing everything to the product level loses the detail operations actually need.

questions.q: What does the brand-category-subcategory-product hierarchy drive, besides organizing the catalog?
options: E-commerce navigation, reporting roll-ups, and category-level tax or regulatory rules
Nothing beyond internal record-keeping — it has no downstream effect
Only the order in which products are manufactured
The customer's billing address format
questions.explain: The hierarchy is functional: shoppers navigate it, reports roll up sales by category through it, and some tax and regulatory rules apply at the category level.

questions.q: What example does this lesson give of a mismatched unit of measure causing a costly error?
options: An order for 10 cases being fulfilled as an order for 10 individual units
A product being listed in the wrong currency
A SKU barcode failing to scan at checkout
A product category being renamed without notice
questions.explain: If the product master and a warehouse system disagree on unit of measure, an order meant for 10 cases can be fulfilled as 10 individual units — an expensive, preventable error.
